title: What Is a Copay? How Copays Work in Health Insurance
summary: What is a copay? Learn how copays work, how they differ from deductibles and coinsurance, whether they count toward your out-of-pocket max, and examples.
body_markdown:
If you've ever looked at a medical bill or your insurance card, you've probably seen a copay listed. But what does it actually mean for your wallet, and how does it fit into the bigger picture of your health plan? This guide explains what a copay is, how copays interact with deductibles and coinsurance, and how to plan for them.


## Quick answer: What is a copay or copayment?


A copay or copayment is a fixed amount you pay for a covered health care service at the time you receive it. If your health insurance plan lists a $25 copay for a primary care doctor visit, you pay that $25 at the doctor's office when you check in. Copays are a set dollar amount rather than a percentage of the bill, which makes them predictable.


A copay is one part of cost sharing in a health insurance plan. Cost sharing also includes your[deductible](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-deductible) (the amount you pay before your insurance company begins covering its share) and[coinsurance](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) (a percentage of costs you pay after meeting your deductible). Together, these determine how you and your insurer split health care costs.


You'll see copays in common situations: a primary care provider visit, a specialist appointment, urgent care, the emergency room, or when you pick up prescription drugs at a pharmacy. Copays are paid at the time of service. Depending on your health plan, copays may or may not count toward your deductible, but they generally count toward your yearly out-of-pocket maximum.[HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/co-payment/) defines a copay as "a fixed amount you pay for a covered health care service."


## How do copays work with your health insurance?


Copays are one way you share health care costs with your insurer under most individual, employer, and marketplace insurance plans. Your insurance policy spells out how copays work for different services, so the amount you pay is set before the plan year begins.


Your copay amounts are listed in your plan documents (the Summary of Benefits and Coverage) and often printed on your health insurance ID card. You might see something like "PCP: $25, Specialist: $50, ER: $300." These are fixed amounts, not percentages. The copay amount doesn't change based on how long the visit lasted. Lab tests your doctor orders during the appointment may be billed separately.


Copay amounts vary by service type and insurance plan. Your plan may charge a lower copay for a primary care doctor visit than for a specialist. Urgent care and emergency room copays usually differ from each other. Telehealth visits may carry lower copays than in-person visits. Prescription copays often depend on whether you fill a generic or brand-name medication. Copays can also differ for[in-network and out-of-network providers](https://www.withflex.com/blog/in-network-vs-out-of-network) , and many plans charge lower copays when you use in-network doctors.


Here's a quick scenario. Imagine you have a 2026 employer health plan with a $20 copay for a primary care visit and a $10 copay for generic prescriptions. You see your doctor on Monday for a cough and pay $20 at check-in. On Wednesday, you pick up the generic antibiotic your doctor prescribed and pay $10 at the pharmacy. That week, your total copay costs are $30, regardless of where your deductible balance stands.


## Copay vs. deductible vs. coinsurance: What's the difference?


These are the three main types of cost sharing in health care. They work together over a plan year, but each plays a different role, and understanding how they interact can prevent billing surprises.


- **Deductible:** the amount you pay before your plan starts paying its share for most covered services.
- **Copay:** a fixed fee for services like an office visit or a prescription fill.
- **Coinsurance:** a percentage of costs you pay after the deductible is met.


In short: copay = flat fee, coinsurance = percentage. Our guide to[what coinsurance is](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-coinsurance) compares copay vs. coinsurance in more detail.


Here's how they usually interact. Suppose your health plan has a $2,000 annual deductible, a $30 copay for primary care visits, and 20% coinsurance for hospital and imaging services. When you visit your primary care doctor, you pay a $30 copay even if you haven't met your deductible. If you later need an MRI costing $1,000 and you've already met your deductible, you pay 20% coinsurance ($200) and the health plan pays the remaining $800. In some plans, copays apply before you meet your deductible; in others, copays only kick in after. This is plan-specific, so always check your documents.


An out-of-pocket maximum caps what you spend on covered in-network services in a year. Your[out-of-pocket maximum](https://www.withflex.com/blog/deductible-vs-out-of-pocket-maximum) includes deductibles, copays, and coinsurance. For 2026, the ACA caps it at $10,600 for an individual and $21,200 for a family. Once you reach it, your plan pays 100% of covered in-network services for the rest of the plan year. Your monthly[premium](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-premium) doesn't count toward the deductible or the out-of-pocket max.


## What services typically have a copay?


Not every covered service has a copay, but many everyday health care services do. Common services that carry copays under most plans include:


- Primary care doctor visits for routine or non-emergency issues
- Specialist visits (dermatologist, cardiologist, OB-GYN)
- Urgent care or retail clinic visits
- Emergency room visits (usually the highest copay)
- Mental health counseling or therapy sessions
- Prescription drugs at the pharmacy


Copay amounts are often tiered. You'll typically pay a lower copay for a primary care visit than for a specialist or emergency care. Prescription copays usually follow drug tiers. For example, a plan might charge $10 for a generic medication, $50 for a preferred brand-name drug, and $100 for a non-preferred brand.


Some imaging, lab tests, or outpatient procedures may have separate copays or may be subject to your deductible instead, depending on how your plan categorizes them. Not all health plans handle these services the same way.


## What services may not require a copay?


Under the Affordable Care Act, most health plans must cover certain[preventive services](https://www.healthcare.gov/coverage/preventive-care-benefits/) without cost sharing when you use an in-network provider, even if you haven't met your deductible. This applies to non-grandfathered plans.


Preventive services that typically have a $0 copay include annual checkups with your primary care doctor, childhood vaccines, many adult immunizations like the flu shot, and certain cancer screenings such as mammograms and colonoscopies when done as routine preventive care.


There's an important distinction: if a visit is coded as diagnostic rather than preventive, because you came in with symptoms rather than for a routine screening, normal copays, deductibles, or coinsurance can apply. The billing code matters. High-deductible health plans can also cover certain care for chronic conditions before you meet the deductible, but this varies by plan.


Check your Summary of Benefits and Coverage or your insurer's website to confirm which services in your plan have no copay.


## Do copays count toward your deductible and out-of-pocket maximum?


This is really two separate questions, and the answers are usually different.


In many plans, copays don't count toward your deductible. Your deductible is met through other covered costs like hospital stays, imaging, or lab work, and the copays you pay for doctor visits or prescriptions don't reduce it. Some plans do count copays toward the deductible, so check yours.


Copays do count toward your out-of-pocket maximum. HealthCare.gov defines the out-of-pocket limit as including "deductibles, copayments, and coinsurance." Here's a worked example: Maria has a plan with a $1,500 deductible and a $5,000 out-of-pocket max. She visits her primary care doctor four times in a year, paying a $30 copay each time, or $120 total. Those copays don't reduce her $1,500 deductible, but they do count toward her out-of-pocket maximum, bringing her remaining cap down to $4,880.


Plan designs vary, so confirm in your plan booklet or online portal. And remember: your monthly premium doesn't count toward your deductible or out-of-pocket maximum.


## Copays in different plan types: traditional plans vs. high-deductible plans


Plan design affects when and how copays apply. The two most common structures are traditional plans (an[HMO or PPO](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hmo-vs-ppo) ) and high-deductible health plans (HDHPs).


Traditional[PPO](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-is-a-ppo) or HMO plans often have predictable copays for doctor visits and prescriptions from the first day of coverage. You pay a copay each time you see your doctor or a specialist or fill a prescription. Many people find these plans easier to budget for because the copay amount is known in advance. The trade-off is usually a higher monthly premium, along with lower deductibles and more services covered by a flat fee before the deductible.


High-deductible plans work differently. The deductible is higher, and you often pay the full cost of services until you reach it. Some HDHPs have few or no copays until you've met your deductible, while others charge copays for certain services after the deductible. HDHPs typically come with a lower premium, and they can be paired with a Health Savings Account (HSA), per[IRS Publication 969](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p969) . For 2026, an HSA-qualified HDHP must have a deductible of at least $1,700 for self-only coverage or $3,400 for family coverage.


Consider two coworkers in 2026. One enrolls in a traditional plan with a higher monthly premium but pays $20 per primary care visit and $10 for generic drugs. The other chooses a high-deductible health plan with a lower premium, a $2,500 deductible, and no copays until that deductible is met. Which one pays less overall depends on how much care each person uses during the year. Our[PPO vs. HDHP comparison](https://www.withflex.com/blog/ppo-vs-hdhp) walks through how to choose.


## Real-life examples: How copays work in everyday care


These scenarios show how copays work alongside deductibles and coinsurance in typical situations.


**Example: Routine primary care visit.** John has a plan with a $500 deductible, a $25 copay for primary care, and a $4,000 out-of-pocket max. He sees his doctor for a sinus infection and pays $25 at check-in. If his doctor orders a strep test, the lab charge may apply toward his deductible separately. The $25 copay doesn't reduce his deductible balance, but it counts toward his out-of-pocket maximum.


**Example: Specialist visit and imaging.** Ana is referred to an orthopedist. Her plan has a $50 specialist copay, a $1,200 deductible, and 20% coinsurance for imaging. She pays $50 at the specialist's office. When the orthopedist orders an MRI costing $1,000, that charge applies to her deductible first. If she still owes $700 on her deductible, she pays that $700 in full, then 20% coinsurance on the remaining $300 ($60). The copay and the deductible and coinsurance payments all count toward her out-of-pocket max.


**Example: Prescription drugs.** Sarah's plan has a $10 copay for generic drugs, $50 for preferred brand-name drugs, and $100 for non-preferred brands. She fills a generic and a preferred brand in one month, paying $60 total in prescription copays. Those payments count toward her out-of-pocket maximum. Whether they count toward her deductible depends on her plan's rules.


## Paying copays with an HSA or FSA


Many people use tax-advantaged accounts to pay out-of-pocket costs, including copays. If you have an[HSA or FSA](https://www.withflex.com/blog/what-are-hsas-fsas) , you can use it to pay for qualified medical expenses with pre-tax dollars.


A Health Savings Account is available to people enrolled in a qualifying high-deductible health plan. A Flexible Spending Account is an employer-sponsored account that lets you set aside pre-tax money for health care costs within the plan year. Under[IRS Publication 502](https://www.irs.gov/publications/p502) , amounts you pay for medical care that insurance doesn't reimburse, including copays, deductibles, and coinsurance, are qualified medical expenses.


You can use an HSA or FSA card at a clinic or pharmacy to pay the copay directly, or pay out of pocket and then request[reimbursement](https://www.withflex.com/blog/hsa-fsa-reimbursement-how-to) from your account administrator. Contribution limits change each year, so check the current IRS limits and your plan's rules.


## How to estimate and manage your yearly copay costs


Understanding your copays can help you budget for annual health care costs and compare plans during[open enrollment](https://www.withflex.com/blog/your-2026-open-enrollment-cheat-sheet-7-terms-you-actually-need-to-know) . A simple approach gives you a rough yearly estimate.


Start by looking up each copay amount in your Summary of Benefits and Coverage or on your ID card. Then estimate how many times in a typical year you expect to use each service, such as two primary care visits, one specialist visit, and twelve monthly prescription fills for a family member on ongoing medication. Multiply expected visits by their copay amounts. If your primary care copay is $30 and you expect four visits, that's $120 in copays for that service alone.


Check whether copays change after you've met your deductible or after you reach your out-of-pocket max. Many insurers offer online cost estimators and portals that track how much you've paid and how much remains before you hit your out-of-pocket maximum.


If any part of how copays, deductibles, and coinsurance interact is confusing, contact your insurer's member services, your HR benefits office, or trusted resources like[HealthCare.gov](https://www.healthcare.gov/glossary/co-payment/) and[KFF](https://www.kff.org/private-insurance/navigating-the-maze-a-look-at-patient-cost-sharing-complexities-and-consumer-protections/) . Knowing what your insurance pays, and what you owe, puts you in a stronger position to manage your health care spending year-round.
